titolo: LTCM – The Nobel Genius Fund That Lost $4.6 Billion
descrizione:
In 1994, a hedge fund staffed by Wall Street traders and two future Nobel laureates promised steady, low-risk profits. Four years later, Long-Term Capital Management had lost $4.6 billion in a matter of months and was rescued under the supervision of the New York Fed. This video investigates how the fund's leverage, its trading strategy and the 1998 Russian default combined into a near-systemic crisis.

We walk through the timeline from the fund's launch in 1994 to the September 1998 bailout, explain the mechanism of leveraged convergence trades in plain language, and look at what the episode taught regulators and investors. Sources include the President's Working Group report (1999), congressional testimony and major newspaper coverage from 1998.

fatti: Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM) lost about $4.6 billion in 1998
On September 23, 1998 the New York Fed organized a rescue by 14 financial institutions
The 14 firms put in about $3.65 billion in total
Open question: how did a fund run by Nobel laureates fail so badly that the Fed stepped in?
LTCM was founded in 1994 by John Meriwether, former vice chairman and head of bond arbitrage at Salomon Brothers
Partners included Myron Scholes and Robert Merton, who shared the 1997 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
Another partner was David Mullins, former Vice Chairman of the Federal Reserve
The fund started trading in early 1994 with roughly $1.25 billion in capital
Based in Greenwich, Connecticut
Core strategy: convergence or relative-value arbitrage, betting that small price gaps between similar bonds would narrow
Each trade earned only a tiny spread
To make those spreads meaningful, LTCM used heavy leverage
Returns after fees were reported at about 43% in 1995 and 41% in 1996 and about 17% in 1997
Investors were charged high fees, about 2% of assets and 25% of profits
At the end of 1997 LTCM returned about $2.7 billion to outside investors, keeping the leverage higher relative to its capital
At the start of 1998 LTCM had about $4.7 billion in equity
It held assets of more than $120 billion, a leverage ratio of roughly 25 to 1
Off-balance-sheet derivatives positions had a notional value of about $1.25 trillion
Notional value is not the same as the amount at risk
On August 17, 1998 Russia devalued the ruble and defaulted on its domestic debt
Investors fled to safe assets such as US Treasury bonds, widening the spreads LTCM had bet would narrow
LTCM lost about $550 million on August 21, 1998, according to the President's Working Group report
In August 1998 the fund lost about 44% of its capital
Its models had not accounted for such a correlated global flight to safety
By late September 1998 LTCM's equity had fallen to about $400 million, per the 1999 President's Working Group report
Counterparties demanded more collateral as losses mounted
The fund's positions were so large that selling them risked moving markets further
Meriwether sought outside capital, including approaches to Warren Buffett's group, which did not result in a deal
On September 23, 1998 William McDonough, president of the New York Fed, convened leaders of major banks at the New York Fed
The Fed did not put in its own money; it brokered the private rescue
14 firms contributed about $3.65 billion in exchange for roughly 90% of the fund
On September 29, 1998 the Fed cut the federal funds rate by 0.25 percentage points, the first of three cuts that autumn
The concern was the risk of disorderly liquidation across global markets
The consortium unwound the portfolio over the following months
By early 1999 the creditors had been repaid with a profit, according to reports at the time
The fund was formally dissolved in early 2000
Congress held hearings on October 1, 1998 on hedge fund risk
The President's Working Group on Financial Markets issued a report on hedge funds, leverage and the lessons of LTCM in April 1999

Answer to the opening question: heavy leverage of about 25 to 1, huge positions and models assuming normal market conditions left the fund exposed when the Russian default triggered a global flight to safety
Risk models are only as good as their assumptions
Liquidity can vanish exactly when it is needed
Size and interconnection can make a private failure a public problem
End with: Subscribe for the next one.

_correzioni: Title/description/cover/chapter 1: 'lost $4.6 billion in a matter of months' is OK for 1998, but 'in four months' is imprecise (losses mostly May–September 1998); changed cover 'LOST IN FOUR MONTHS' to 'LOST IN 1998'
Description: 'two future Nobel laureates' fixed to 'two future Nobel laureates' is correct (Scholes and Merton won in 1997, after the 1994 launch), kept; 'Four years later' kept
Founding: Meriwether was vice chairman of Salomon Brothers and head of bond arbitrage; kept. Starting capital about $1.25 billion kept
Fees: 2% of assets and 25% of profits kept
End 1997: returned about $2.7 billion to investors, leaving about $4.7 billion equity at start of 1998; kept
Assets: over $120 billion and notional derivatives about $1.25 trillion kept; leverage 'roughly 25 to 1' kept

Aug 21, 1998 loss of $550 million kept per PWG report; 'lost about 44% in August' changed to 'about 44% of its value in August 1998' retained as documented (equity fell from about $2.9bn to about $2.1bn in August is ~44%? uncertain) so reworded to 'lost about 44% of its capital in August'
Equity by late September about $400 million kept (PWG)
Bailout date: the consortium deal was finalized Sept 23, 1998 (meeting at NY Fed, McDonough convened); 'convened leaders' kept
Consortium: 14 firms contributed $3.65 billion for 90% stake kept
Fed rate cut: first cut was Sept 29, 1998 by 0.25 points, followed by cuts on Oct 15 and Nov 17; kept
Congressional hearing: House Banking Committee hearing was October 1, 1998; kept
Dissolution: fund was liquidated and closed in early 2000; kept
